newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Olivetti makes first step to health.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Olivetti makes first step to health.

text.p: Italy's Olivetti has taken a big step towards recovery with the sell-off of its loss-making personal computers but the hi-tech group still faces a struggle to overcome margin pressures and high debts.

Olivetti completed the planned sale of its PC company on Monday, pushing forward chief executive Roberto Colaninno's restructuring plan but analysts on Tuesday were still concerned about poor trading and prospects of a rights issue at end-1997.
"This is certainly a major step as it reduces the risk profile of the company by extracting Olivetti from a highly volatile market," said one industry analyst in London.

But many were withholding judgement on the deal as the details of the buying consortium Piedmont International were not fully known, nor was the exact trading relationship between the new company and Olivetti's remaining businesses.
Olivetti shares responded positively to the sale and at 1210 GMT were up 3.18 percent at 685 lire in a lower Milan market.

Colaninno announced Monday Olivetti would gain 250-300 billion lire ($160-190 million) from the sale of its PCs to the Piedmont group of domestic and international investors brought together by Edward Gottesman, the U.S. lawyer behind the Centenary group. Olivetti will hold 10 percent of Piedmont.

Most analysts said that the deal was probably the best Colaninno could deliver, and at least he had delivered on a promise he made last October after a series of broken promises that litter Olivetti's past history.
Analysts said a key factor in the success of the deal will be an agreement between Piedmont and Olivetti's systems and service unit on PCs sales and prices between the two.
"Colaninno has shown a strong approach towards strategy at the group," said Paola Toschi at brokers Milla, adding that investors can start to consider a recovery in the core group.

She expects net debt at the group to fall to around 1.7 trillion lire by March after the deal is completed and said the group's debt-equity ratio would fall to around 100 percent. The company's net debt was 2.916 trillion lire at end-November.
"We are now through the emergency phase, well into the disposal phase, but now comes the revitalisation phase," said the London-based analyst.

Colaninno who took over last September is faced with the problem of two emerging telecoms businesses that are still absorbing cash and making losses, while its other three businesses PCs, systems and services and Lexikon office equipment have seen trading conditions deteriorate.

His strategy was to make 800 billion lire of disposals in 1996 -- now largely accounted for by the sale of a 5.6 percent stake in Omnitel and PCs -- and then 400 billion lire in 1997 likely to be met by a partial float of Lexikon.

Analysts say his hands are being tied as banks will not roll-over all their debts at Olivetti so the immediate sell-offs are needed to bring debt down. But then cash will be needed to push the group forward, and Colaninno has said that a rights issue may be needed at the end of this year.

Analysts said PCs were a problem but not the only one as they point out that the PC company made a 10 billion lire operating loss in the first half of 1996 while the group as a whole made a 81 billion lire first half loss.

Its telecoms businesses, 35.5 percent-owned mobile phone consortium Omnitel and fixed-line telecoms company Telemedia, are still in a start-up phases and made losses, while its core systems and services business and office equipment company Lexikon both saw margins and profits decline in the first half. ($1=1,576 lire)
